newsitem.title: UK: Mark hit as market bets on political push for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Mark hit as market bets on political push for EMU.

text.p: The mark lost ground to its European satellites on Friday as the market grew ever more convinced that political will would triumph over economic realities and usher in a broad, soft single European currency.

With agreement now in sight on the key EU budget stability pact and officials laying stress on sustainable convergence rather than splitting hairs over entry criteria, players bet on the timely launch of a weak euro and sold marks.
But analysts said fears of EMU delay were not dead and could return to haunt the market sooner rather than later.

"Our feeling is people just want to believe in a soft EMU. We still think there's a very good chance of postponement round the corner -- and the mark will get whipsawed like there's no tomorrow," said David Bloom, economist at HSBC James Capel.
The mark slipped to 982.00/30 Italian lire and 3.3728/31 French francs by 0808 GMT from late Thursday's European levels of 983.25/55 and 3.3745/50.

That was well down from the highs of 991.55 and 3.3843 hit this week after France's request for more time to study the stability pact, which is designed to enforce budgetary rigour after EMU begins, ignited concerns that the whole project would be delayed.
Those fears have been gradually allayed, however, by signs that a compromise is evolving to allow the pact to be signed, as scheduled, at the Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.

EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the pact would be formally adopted in Amsterdam and would include extra resolutions on employment and policy coordination -- key demands of France's new Socialist-led government.
EU Commission President Jacques Santer predicted a deal, if Europe stepped up the fight for jobs and policy coordination.
Friday's focus was on a summit between German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and France's president and prime minister.

"With today's Franco-German summit likely to produce some positive rhetoric, I can't see the high-yielding currencies coming under any downward pressure," said James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber in London.

But the risk of a clash between France and Germany remains, analysts warned. The new French government is to audit public finances and present a mini-budget, while Germany's ruling coalition is still discussing how to reduce its budget deficit.
"It's quite clear the French Socialist government is not going to be taking further austerity measures," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.
"If we do see an expansionary mini-budget in France, that's likely to be badly received by the German government," he added.
For now, though, officials are keen to stress their harmony and their unshakeable will to see EMU proceed as planned.

An OECD report out Thursday which predicted Germany, France and Italy would all have budget deficits of 3.2 percent of GDP in 1997 -- above the EMU target of 3.0 -- sparked a chorus of reassuring comments from politicians and central bankers.
Bundesbank head Hans Tietmeyer said sustainability was more important than exact figures, while his Dutch counterpart Wim Duisenberg said a 3.2 percent deficit would be no catastrophe.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said three percent was not a "knockout" criterion for EMU participation, and German finance minister Theo Waigel said he did not wish to engage in a discussion on decimal points, saying credibility was key.
"It clearly shows politics are still driving EMU," said DKB's Stamenkovic.
Still, there are serious doubts whether the will is there to include Italy in the first round of EMU in 1999.
While the OECD foresaw the French and German deficits falling to meet EMU targets in 1998, the Italian shortfall was seen ballooning to 3.8 percent.
Tietmeyer said, however, that Italy had the same chance as every country to join monetary union, and insisted Germany was not opposed to Italian participation.
That helped weaken the mark as it sharpened market anticipation of a broad, soft euro.
But with Italy apparently on course to fall way short of the entry targets, analysts suggested Tietmeyer had little to lose by making such encouraging noises.
